description: Hey y'all. We're a group of friends in grade 12 who aspire to pursue STEM careers like engineering and computer science. We all have joint experience with C# through Visual Studio Community in the ICS3 and 4U courses, and with Python from Grade 10 via VS Code. We all have experience making fun games from scratch using WinForms and look forward to building a good project for our challenge :)
summary: Space Design Game is a rocket-building and mission planning game where players design rockets from modular parts, manage budgets, and launch their creations. Players control throttle, pitch, and fuel during atmospheric flight, then navigate orbital mechanics to intercept planets for surface landings and science sample collection. The game features crew roles with unique perks, connection-validated assembly, real gravitational physics, and seamless transitions between atmospheric, orbital, and surface flight. It combines engineering design with space exploration.
details:
The project uses C# with .NET Framework, and WinForms for the UI. It features real gravitational physics, crew role perks, connection-validated rocket assembly, and procedural terrain generation.

Benefits The game shows how much planning goes into a space mission. Every choice has a cost, whether it’s money, weight or crew. Players also pick up basic ideas like thrust to weight ratio, fuel use and power management without reading a textbook. Intended impact We want to make people curious about space and engineering. We hope players come away understanding that real missions depend on tradeoffs and teamwork, and that some of them get interested in STEM careers. Tools and technology -Language: C# -Framework: .NET Framework 4.7.2 with Windows Forms -Graphics: GDI+ (System.Drawing). The cockpit, gauges and space views are drawn in code -Software: Visual Studio


What makes it creative:
The creativity is shown in the creation of the rocket in the hangar where the player can make their rocket how they want and it actually affects how the rocket travels due to gravity and thrust vs mass.


What we considered:

Parts and crew had to be costly enough that choices matter, but not so costly that players feel stuck. We simplified the physics so it feels believable but stays playable. The game has drag and drop building, an instructions screen and clear on-screen warnings. The game draws only what’s on screen, so it runs smoothly even at huge altitudes. All of this was done by splitting up the work, testing each other’s code and fixing bugs together.
